article:
## Definition
Geospatial digital solutions are the applications and platforms that deliver spatial data to the people who need it in their daily work, in a form suited to their role: interactive maps and dashboards for decision-makers, web applications for staff and the public, field apps for operational teams, and enterprise portals and platforms that bring all of this together. Their value lies in moving spatial data off specialists' computers and into users' hands.

## Categories
By user, these solutions fall into desktop solutions for specialists, web applications for staff and the public, field apps that run on mobile devices even without a connection, and dashboards for senior management. By architecture, they fall into on-premises solutions, cloud solutions, and hybrid solutions that combine the two. One of the newest patterns is the digital twin: a 3D digital model of a city or facility linked to its operational data.

## Methodology
Building a solution starts by analyzing workflows and users before any technology: who will use the solution, for which task, and what data they need. Then comes user experience design, the solution architecture and its integration with the organization's existing systems, followed by iterative development through prototypes that users test early, and finally deployment, training, and support. Throughout, the solution follows open interoperability standards, such as those of the OGC, to avoid lock-in to a single product.

## A brief history
In the 1980s and 1990s, geographic information systems remained desktop tools used only by specialists, and they began moving to the web at the turn of the millennium. In 2005, the launch of Google Maps changed what users expected from online maps, making ease of use a core requirement. With the spread of smart devices equipped with GPS, field data collection moved from paper to apps, and updates began reaching the database the moment they were entered.

## Business impact
When spatial data reaches users at the right time and in the right form, it turns from a stockpile into a working tool: the need for files and paper maps falls, data is updated directly from the field, departments share a single view of assets and services, and decision-makers follow indicators in real time instead of waiting for periodic reports.

## Use cases
A spatial services portal lets residents submit a request, mark its location on the map, and follow it up. A field app enables maintenance teams to inventory assets and update their condition with photos and coordinates. An executive dashboard brings performance indicators together on a single map that reveals where problems are concentrated.

## Why it matters
The value of spatial data is realized only when it is used, and digital solutions are the bridge that turns an organization's investment in data into daily work, faster decisions, and better services.

cases.title: A spatial services portal for a municipality
cases.challenge: Requests and reports arriving through multiple channels without a precise location, making them hard to route and follow up.
cases.approach: A web portal where users mark the location on a map, linked to the request management system and neighborhood data.
cases.result: Requests with precise locations, faster dispatch of teams, and a spatial view of how requests are distributed.

cases.title: A field app for asset inventory
cases.challenge: A paper-based asset inventory that is entered late and full of errors.
cases.approach: An offline-capable mobile app that records location, photos, and condition, and syncs with the database.
cases.result: An asset register updated directly from the field, with fewer data entry errors.

cases.title: An executive dashboard for tracking spatial indicators
cases.challenge: Late periodic reports that don't show where problems are concentrated.
cases.approach: A dashboard that links indicators to the map and updates automatically from the data sources.
cases.result: Real-time tracking of indicators, and decisions based on a clear spatial picture.
